items.abstract_or_text: Large language models (LLMs) deployed in mental-health contexts can be evaluated for safety failures, but the resulting judgments are often difficult to inspect or explain. Common approaches to improving safety rely on prompt engineering, LLM-as-a-Judge, and Constitutional AI. In this work, we describe a clinician-led alternative in which two clinicians define, finalize, and adjudicate the four safety checks of a rule base, which is formally verified for internal consistency and applied as a guardrail over LLM outputs. Here and in the title, clinician-led refers to this rule base, not to the fact extractor or the uncertainty default, which are ours. Every verdict of the resulting verification layer is recomputable from a named rule and sixteen facts. Against an LLM judge matched in model, revision, quantization, rule text, and decoding but without the layer's computed 988/911 fact, the largest disagreement class, the satisfied-rule class, is structured: the Llama-3.3-70B judge, on its primary prompt, demands a crisis resource from 55 of the 65 replies (84.6%) that already contain one, while the same model, asked as a fact extractor, reports a recognized resource present on 54 of the 55. The verification layer never raises that demand, by construction. We report with equal prominence where this judge is stronger: fewer false crisis alarms on the one reference-scored check. We also report the measured cost (a specification revision raised block-class outcomes on held-out boundary prompts of an over-refusal benchmark from 6.0% to 16.0%, chiefly by changing fact extraction), the clinicians' decision to keep our uncertainty default, and the analysis of the result. The contribution is not a safer verdict. It is a guardrail whose disagreements with the judge localize to named rules and facts and whose measured costs trace to named facts and the uncertainty default.

items.title: kinGEMs: A Robust and Scalable Framework for Resource-Constraint Models through Stochastic Tuning of Deep Learning-Predicted Kinetic Parameters
items.abstract_or_text: The construction of accurate enzyme-constrained genome-scale models (ecGEMs) remains a critical challenge in systems biology, limited by sparse kinetic data and the need for biologically meaningful representations. This work presents an integrated framework combining CPI-Pred, a deep learning model to predict kinetic parameters (kcat) from sequence and compound embeddings, with kinGEMs, a pipeline to incorporate these uncertainty-aware parameters into ecGEMs for metabolic optimization. By leveraging representations at multiple scales, the approach captures sequence, structure, and kinetic data to enhance model generalizability and accuracy. Rigorous benchmarking demonstrates the framework's capability to predict growth rates and fluxes that are consistent with experimental observations and measured proteome fractions, reduce median flux variability by several folds, and yield better-constrained metabolic models by explicitly accounting for the uncertainty inherent in ML-predicted kinetic parameters. kinGEMs successfully generated ecGEMs for 93 models spanning a phylogenetically diverse set of organisms including Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacteria, mycobacteria, parasitic protists, fungi, and mammalian cell lines. These innovations breakdown the barrier to application of ecGEMs to non-model organisms and open new avenues for metabolic engineering and synthetic biology in more industrially relevant hosts.

items.title: Aclarubicin disrupts RNA polymerase II progression at replication-coupled histone genes
items.abstract_or_text: Anthracyclines are effective chemotherapeutic agents that cause DNA and chromatin damage. One member of the anthracyclines, aclarubicin, has gained therapeutic interest due to its ability to kill cancer cells through chromatin-based mechanisms, thus avoiding the off-target effects associated with DNA damage. However, the molecular mechanism of action leading to aclarubicin-induced chromatin damage remains elusive. Here we performed Cleavage Under Targets and Tagmentation (CUT&Tag) of RNA polymerase II (Pol II) and other transcriptional regulators in human cells followin aclarubicin treatment. We found that aclarubicin strongly disrupts the replication-coupled histone genes, resulting in a nonproductive accumulation of Pol II transcription machinery here beyond the levels at other genes. We attribute this sensitivity to the dense Pol II loading and rapid transcription of the histone genes, which intensify the chromatin-disrupting effects of aclarubicin. Together, our findings shed light on the mechanism of aclarubicin as an anticancer drug and point to the replication-coupled histone genes as a target for therapeutic intervention.

items.title: Decision-only medical AI: early evidence and pairing with language models
items.abstract_or_text: Recently introduced decision-only AI returns probabilities over specified options rather than text. We tested the clinical consistency and potential bias susceptibility of the two available decision models, Jev and OpenAI Decisions, against a large language model (LLM), GPT-6 Luna, then paired each decision model with the LLM. Across 2,134 case presentations and 2,483,222 model calls, we measured decision changes after adding labels or pressure cues without changing clinical findings. In the original controlled challenges, these additions changed 13.4 more decisions per 100 than neutral wording for the decision models and 14.0 for the LLM. Pairing reduced this to 2.6, about 81% lower in development and 42% to 48% lower in held-out reports. Triage accuracy stayed near 81% to 82%. The paired Decisions workflow cost at most US0.77 per 1,000 entries. We see this as a practical proof of concept for reducing framing sensitivity and flagging influential text for review.

items.title: Reference-free and robust copy number inference in single-cell tumor transcriptomes
items.abstract_or_text: Copy number changes are a hallmark of cancer and reveal which cells are malignant and how tumors evolve. Single-cell RNA sequencing is widely used to infer them in individual tumor cells. Existing methods do so by normalizing each cell against a reference of normal cells. As a result, their output depends on which cells are analyzed together, they often label normal cells as aneuploid, and they struggle in samples without normal cells. Here we present REFCON, a deep-learning model that infers copy number from each cell's own expression, without a reference. We evaluated REFCON on more than 410,000 held-out cells from cell lines, organoids and 112 tumors of nine cancer types, profiled with seven sequencing technologies. It agreed more closely with single-cell DNA than existing methods, was unaffected by sample composition, and labeled far fewer normal cells as aneuploid. In patient-derived organoids, which contain no normal cells, it gave consistent profiles across passages and tracked clonal evolution. REFCON addresses long-standing limitations of reference-based inference and enables robust, reference-free copy number calling from single-cell transcriptomes.

items.title: MAMBAxBrain: A Multi-task Neural Framework Linking Brain Functional Dynamics to Individual Fingerprints, Cognitive and Disease States
items.abstract_or_text: Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) contains rich individual, cognitive, and pathological information, yet no universal model exists for multi-task modeling of these dimensions. Here, we introduce MAMBAxBrain, a multitask neural framework that integrates Mamba architecture with functional connectivity analysis to jointly model the temporal dynamics and spatial coordination of neural activity. MAMBAxBrain achieves high accuracy across four distinct fMRI objectives, including brain fingerprinting, cognitive task decoding, reaction time prediction, and schizophrenia classification, consistently outperforming state-of-the-art methods with robust cross-session generalization. Interpretability analyses show that each task engages distinct, biologically plausible circuitry: from higher-order association cortex for identity to subcortical-motor loops for reaction time and disrupted control-sensory connectivity for schizophrenia. These findings inform a longstanding debate: rather than operating through wholly separate or entirely shared systems, the brain preferentially recruits task-specific circuits while retaining common representational structure across functions.

items.title: Using a lanthanide tagged nanobody to visualise Glial fibrillary acidic protein by secondary ion mass spectrometry
items.abstract_or_text: Lanthanide-labelled antibodies have been widely used for multiplex imaging of proteins directly from tissue using two approaches, imaging mass cytometry (IMC) and variants of secondary ion mass spectrometry (SIMS). Here we show the same approach can be taken using SIMS, but utilising lanthanide-labelled nanobodies instead. Nanobodies offer several advantages over conventional antibodies for antigen tagging, owing to their small size (12-15 kDa), high stability, and solubility. Their reduced molecular size enables greater diffusion through tissue, facilitating access to target sites and allowing them to reach regions that may be less accessible to larger antibodies. This enhanced accessibility can promote more effective localisation and increase binding to target antigens. In the work presented here, we produced a lanthanide-tagged nanobody and assessed its efficacy and compatibility with mass spectrometry imaging (MSI). We showed successful detection of Glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) in tissue by correlating MSI of a lanthanide-tagged anti-GFAP nanobody with immunofluorescence microscopy imaging (IF). The use of nanobodies is an excellent alternative to current antibody tagging methods for SIMS and IMC.

items.title: BUDDY: An interactive web platform to accelerate the functional modeling of human missense variants using Saccharomyces cerevisiae orthologs
items.abstract_or_text: The advent of next-generation sequencing has transformed clinical genetics, accelerating the identification of human genetic variants. However, the labor-intensive process of functional validation of Variants of Uncertain Significance (VUS) remains a significant diagnostic barrier. While expressing humanized genes in Saccharomyces cerevisiae is a common approach for modeling missense variants with functional assays, using native yeast orthologs provides a more streamlined approach that preserves species-specific interactions within multisubunit complexes. However, taking this approach relies on a fragmented workflow that requires bioinformatic experience. To address this issue, we developed the Bioinformatic Utility for Diagnostic Discovery in Yeast (BUDDY), an integrated web platform designed to streamline variant analysis by connecting bioinformatic tools and databases including ClinVar. Features include amino acid alignments, a protein structure viewer that displays a superposition of yeast and human proteins, pathogenicity prediction data, CRISPR-Cas9 reagent design, and yeast phenotypes to provide potential functional assays. The platform also contains an artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted experimental design feature that evaluates the utility of modeling specific variant and gene combinations in yeast and can assist with phenotype selection. BUDDY significantly accelerated the bioinformatic preparation time needed for ortholog variant modeling by an experienced biologist. Additionally, without prior bioinformatics training, a first-year medical student used BUDDY to develop a self-directed project and proposed a study of five Lynch syndrome-associated VUS using a forward mutation rate assay. BUDDY is designed to accelerate the investigation of human variants in yeast and has a high potential utility for use in resource-constrained settings such as course-based undergraduate research experiences (CUREs).

items.title: Accretion of novel genetic elements reverses genome erosion and enables host-switching in the deep sea
items.abstract_or_text: Endosymbiont genome erosion is driven by relaxed selection and isolation from free-living relatives' gene pools, and can be stalled by horizontal transmission events, but it remains unknown whether genome erosion can be reversed. The chemosynthetic gammaproteobacterial symbionts of deep-sea clams in the family Vesicomyidae offer a useful test case for whether eroded symbiont genomes can acquire novel functional content. Despite having some of the smallest genomes among marine endosymbionts, several lines of evidence, including divergent 16S rRNA variants within hosts, host-switching in sympatry, and phylogenetic signatures of repeated host transitions, suggest these symbionts retain more environmental exposure and evolutionary flexibility than expected under strict vertical transmission. Here, we use comparative genomics across the vesicomyid symbionts to test for evidence of functional gene gain. We find that three lineages have each independently expanded their genomes by approximately 25% relative to close relatives, with some expansions driven by insertion sequence (IS) or phage acquisition. The genomes that contain IS elements have disrupted genome synteny genome-wide, suggesting that these elements mediated structural rearrangements through ectopic recombination. Most strikingly, the symbiont of a thyasirid clam host, Thyasira sp. Haima SOB, harbors four unusually large (~24-40 kb), highly repetitive genes with structural homology to adhesins found broadly across prokaryotes and eukaryotes. These genes show hallmarks of horizontal acquisition and IS-mediated mobilization, and their predicted export via a Type I secretion system suggests a role in mediating attachment to, or exchange of metabolites across, host cell surfaces. Considering that this symbiont lineage switched from a vesicomyid host to a thyasirid host relatively recently, and thyasirids typically host extracellular symbionts, these adhesins may have been instrumental in this host-switch. Together, these findings provide evidence that genome erosion in intracellular symbionts is not strictly unidirectional, and mobile genetic elements can serve as vectors for functional innovation, potentially enabling adaptation to new hosts and environments even after substantial genome reduction has occurred.

items.title: CausalFund: Causality-Inspired Domain Generalization in Retinal Fundus Imaging for Low-Resource Screening
items.abstract_or_text: Early screening for glaucoma and diabetic retinopathy (DR) is critical to prevent irreversible vision loss, yet remains inaccessible to many underserved populations. However, AI models trained on hospital-grade fundus images often generalize poorly to low-cost images acquired with portable devices such as smartphones. We proposed CausalFund, a causally inspired learning framework for training AI models that enable reliable low resource screening from easily acquired non-clinical images. CausalFund disentangles disease-relevant retinal features from spurious image factors to achieve domain generalizable screening across clinical and nonclinical settings. We integrated CausalFund with seven deep learning backbones for glaucoma and DR screening from portable-device fundus images, including lightweight architectures suitable for on-device deployment. Across diverse experimental settings and image quality conditions, CausalFund improved smartphone-domain AUC for most backbones while maintaining comparable hospital-domain performance, and achieved a more balanced sensitivity-specificity trade-off than baselines. As a model-agnostic framework, CausalFund could be extended to other diseases and low-resource settings characterized by degraded or non-standard imaging.

items.title: Proteomic and functional insights into spinal neuroimmune maladaptation: dual-level modulation of mast cell-neural crosstalk by ultramicronized palmitoylethanolamide
items.abstract_or_text: Abstract Repeated morphine administration drives spinal neuroimmune mechanisms contributing to analgesic tolerance and hyperalgesia. We investigated the contribution of mast cell-derived mediators to spinal neuroinflammation and the homeostatic effects of ultramicronized palmitoylethanolamide (PEA) using rat organotypic spinal cord slice cultures. Slices exposed to morphine were treated with conditioned medium from activated RBL-2H3 mast cells. Mast cell-derived conditioned medium induced a robust neuroinflammatory response, upregulating IL-6, IL-1β, CCL2, and PTX3 expression, and markedly enhancing the release of the pro-nociceptive neuropeptide CGRP. These alterations were accompanied by reduced neuronal marker expression and impaired astrocytic reactivity in the spinal dorsal horn. Notably, upstream mast cell pretreatment with PEA modified their secretory activity, blunting subsequent spinal inflammatory cascades. Quantitative proteomic analysis revealed that conditioned medium derived from PEA-treated RBL-2H3 cells extensively reshaped the spinal microenvironment, rescuing extracellular matrix components (such as collagen VI), downregulating neurodegenerative markers (including SIRT2 and BIN1), and inducing protective regulators like LGALS1. Downstream tissue-level application of ultramicronized PEA directly to the spinal slices replicated these beneficial actions, significantly attenuating inflammatory transcription and CGRP release while restoring neuronal and astrocytic homeostatic profiles. Collectively, these findings suggest that mast cell-derived factors promote spinal neuroimmune maladaptation, which is effectively countered by ultramicronized PEA via a dual-level mechanism acting on both the mast cell secretome and the spinal tissue interface. This integrated approach offers a promising translational strategy to preserve opioid efficacy and mitigate central sensitization.

items.title: Large language models show systematic failures in incorporating evolving medical knowledge
items.abstract_or_text: Medical knowledge evolves as clinical guidelines revise recommendations, yet whether large language models (LLMs) faithfully incorporate such changes remains unclear. We introduce ChronoEvo, comprising 1,709 recommendation-level revisions across 12 forms of medical knowledge change, to distinguish recognition of revised guidance from incorporation into clinical recommendations. In the primary model, 90.8% of responses recognized revisions and 80.2% were clinically correct, but only 58.5% fully incorporated guidance, yielding a 32.3-percentage-point recognition-incorporation gap. This dissociation persisted across 14 models and was corroborated by two clinicians' adjudicated assessment of 300 responses, yielding a 40.3-percentage-point gap in the validation sample. Changes in recommendation strength and patient eligibility were associated with retention of outdated guidance. A revision-salience intervention reduced outdated-content retention and improved clinical correctness but did not significantly improve full incorporation. These findings identify faithful incorporation of evolving medical knowledge as a distinct challenge for clinical LLM reliability, even when updated guideline evidence is available.

items.title: Population-scale drug target and variant prioritization with Varformer
items.abstract_or_text: Human genetic variation is a powerful driver of therapeutic target prioritization, yet current models struggle to aggregate variable numbers of variants per gene and are bottlenecked by the scarcity of validated targets. We present Varformer, a multimodal transformer that uses cross-modal attention to integrate contextual representations of missense variants with gene-level features. Trained via positive-unlabeled learning on clinically validated targets across four genetic ancestry groups, Varformer achieves a precision@20 of 0.95, 0.86, and 0.48 across three benchmarks of increasing difficulty. It surpasses a logistic regression ablation by 20% and DrugnomeAI by 23% on the hardest benchmark. Cross-population rank normalization isolates targets with consistent genetic support across ancestry groups. The variant encoder also scores individual variants. Across 1,164 carrier-variant pairs in Genes & Health, Varformer ranked the known pathogenic variant in the carrier's top 20 in 57% of pairs. Varformer is available as an open-source framework for unified target and variant prioritization.

items.title: Cholesterol Paradox: Multi-point Heart Failure Prediction from Lipid Panels in Electronic Health Records
items.abstract_or_text: In cardiovascular medicine, low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) is the main lipid marker used in routine screening to assess cardiovascular risk and guide preventive treatment and dietary changes. An increasing number of studies have recently documented the cholesterol paradox: patients with or at risk of heart failure (HF) often have unexpectedly low levels of LDL-C despite leading to cardiovascular diseases. This paper examines how well retrospective lipid panel measurements, supplemented with apolipoprotein B (ApoB), can predict an initial heart failure (HF) event in several pre-diagnosis time windows, using age-matched patient data from Electronic Health Records (EHRs). This retrospective study uses lipid profiles from multicenter nationwide EHRs from the All of Us Research Program. We apply machine learning and explainable AI (SHAP) to lipid-based prediction and to interpret cholesterol contributions to the diagnosis of first heart failure (HF). One experiment predicts the diagnosis of HF in 36 months; the other distinguishes HF patients from people who have never been diagnosed with cardiovascular disease. A baseline lipid panel that includes ApoB predicts the first HF event up to 36 months in advance, achieving an AUC of 0.624 in men and 0.627 in women. Compared to a group of the same age without previous cardiovascular disease, a lipid profile including ApoB predicts a first HF event with a substantially higher AUC: 0.937 for men and 0.925 for women. Shapley value analyses suggest that higher triglycerides and lower HDL and LDL levels are linked to subsequent HF events, with LDL appearing as the strongest yet counterintuitive predictor. ApoB ranks second in importance; in males, higher ApoB is associated with a greater risk of HF, unlike LDL. In general, the study highlights an unexpected association with LDL and emphasizes the prognostic utility of sex-specific metabolic indicators (TG, HDL) for HF using routinely collected clinical data.

items.title: Would an LLM Match into a Residency? Uncertainty, Reasoning and Image Use of Open Language Models on the Spanish MIR Examination
items.abstract_or_text: Accuracy on medical examinations is common evidence offered for the clinical use of language models, yet a health system that intends to run an open model on its own hardware needs to know considerably more: whether the model recognizes when it is likely to be wrong, whether medical fine-tuning improves this ability, whether its correct answers rest on sound clinical reasoning, or whether it actually uses the images it is given. We examine these questions for four open models of 8 to 27 billion parameters on the Spanish MIR residency examination, scoring 1,552 questions from eight editions under the exam's own rules. Answering every question, the three larger models would rank among roughly the first 600 to 3,000 candidates, with 41 to 43 specialties still open to them. Abstention, however, never pays, because even their least confident answers are right more often than the 25% break-even. Medical fine-tuning reduced overconfidence at the cost of accuracy, without improving how well confidence separates right from wrong answers. Moreover, 13-38% of correct answers rejected a distractor for a clinically unsound reason that confidence did not reflect, and removing or swapping the provided contextual images left accuracy unchanged.

items.title: RIPPLE: Recovery Internalization through Process-Level Policy Learning and Effect-Aware Credit for Long-Horizon Agentic Coding
items.abstract_or_text: Long-horizon coding agents can observe a failure and generate a plausible critique yet continue along the same incorrect trajectory. We call this the Critique-to-Action Handoff Gap. We introduce RIPPLE, a recovery-oriented training framework that internalizes process-level guidance into a single self-recovering policy. A prefix-only teacher provides evidence-grounded recovery supervision without access to future actions or terminal outcomes. After lightweight distillation, reinforcement learning assigns stage-specific credit to reflection triggering, diagnosis, and corrective action. Local validity signals gate trajectory advantages so that intermediate recovery decisions do not indiscriminately inherit terminal outcomes. Across four repository-level software-engineering benchmarks, RIPPLE improves the base policy by an arithmetic mean of 4.8 score points, with no auxiliary critic at deployment. Controlled ablations isolate the benefits of local, stage-aligned credit, and matched-prefix interventions show that critique semantics affect subsequent correction. Recovery gains concentrate where the prefix contains sufficient diagnostic evidence and the repository state remains reversible within the remaining budget.

items.title: Governance-State Corruption in Long-Term Memory for LLM Agents: A Cross-Model Stress Test
items.abstract_or_text: An LLM agent can retrieve a memory correctly yet use it incorrectly after its validity state changes. We study governance-state corruption: faults that alter which retained records enter model-visible context while stored content and tasks remain fixed. Across six providers, 731 benchmark-grounded bases yield 2,080 matched fault pairs. In offline control-plane checks, corruption changes the operative projection in 96.25% of pairs, while oracle-backed enforcement restores it in 100%. For downstream evaluation, a deterministically selected, non-probability LongMemEval/Memora panel resolves 298 of 300 matched triplets (238 distinct bases). Clean-minus-corrupted contrasts are 40.54 percentage points in LongMemEval binary correctness (95% base-cluster interval [30.32, 50.71]) and 30.60 points in rescaled Memora FAMA ([23.31, 37.69]); both sources also show recovery. OAKS Novel native option parity holds for all 6,714 resolved outputs. Full-cohort frozen-scorer corruption/recovery effects (-27.55/+27.51 points) remain descriptive proxies, not validated native semantic population effects. These bounded findings motivate evaluating memory control-state integrity alongside retrieval accuracy.

items.title: Mouse Neural Organoids Model the Mature In Vivo Synaptic Proteome
items.abstract_or_text: Neural organoids represent a promising approach for modelling neural circuits and neurological disease, yet their utility depends on whether they can recapitulate the molecular complexity of mature brain synapses. Here, we optimized a protocol to generate mature forebrain organoids from mouse embryonic stem cells and used time-resolved proteomics to define the emergence of synaptic proteins during maturation. Using fluorescence-activated synaptosome sorting coupled with mass spectrometry, we quantified the synapse-enriched proteome and found a high correlation with matched in vivo synaptic proteomes. These findings demonstrate that complex mature synaptic molecular architecture is present within an in vitro organoid environment.

items.title: Active Learning framework for Antibody Binding Affinity Prediction
items.abstract_or_text: Antibody engineering campaigns must prioritise variants from large combinatorial libraries under limited assay budgets. We present a Gaussian process (GP) active-learning benchmark for antibody-antigen binding affinity prediction across eight public AbBiBench assays spanning influenza hemagglutinin antibodies CR6261 and CR9114 and AAYL-series scFv libraries against the SARS-CoV-2 Spike HR2 peptide. The framework embeds variable heavy and light (VH/VL) sequences with ESM-2 650M, trains GP surrogates over compressed protein-language-model representations, and evaluates kernel, acquisition, representation, classical featurisation, and labelling-budget choices under a unified budget of 10\% of each full pool with a label-blind seed and a fixed held-out evaluation split. Across the benchmark, Tanimoto+UCB has the highest mean Recall@2\% point estimate among tested kernel-acquisition configurations, achieving 57.8\% mean Recall@2\% across five random seeds (68.3\% when scored against the acquisition-eligible pool), compared with 9.6\% for random selection -- a gap that is significant by a paired Wilcoxon test across datasets (p=0.0078); its point estimate is not significantly different from RQ+UCB or Tanimoto+EI at five seeds. We adopt the continuous Tanimoto kernel of gessner2024. The same configuration recovers the largest fractions of top binders in the influenza libraries (74.2\% on 3gbn\_h1, 82.7\% on 3gbn\_h9, and 84.9\% on 4fqi\_h3) while exposing harder AAYL combinatorial landscapes where recall remains lower and more variable. An additional three-seed representation ablation, run under the original protocol and not repeated after the evaluation corrections, ranked ESM-2 650M highest (mean Recall@2\% 0.673 \pm 0.28) among ProtBert, AntiBERTy, AbLang2, ProGen2, and classical encodings. On BindingGYM, the same configuration matches or exceeds ALLM-Ab on two of three datasets using the 100-sample held-out test metric. Structure-mapped Integrated Gradients and KernelSHAP analyses recover CDR-region attribution patterns consistent with contact-derived paratope geometry, though threshold-free (AUROC) analysis shows this qualitative agreement is not matched by strong residue-level discrimination. These results support Tanimoto-kernel GP active learning as a simple, reproducible strategy for label-efficient antibody affinity optimisation with qualitative structural validation.

items.title: An Interpretable Machine Learning Framework for Early- versus Late-Stage Classification of Breast Cancer from Gene Expression, with Co-expression Network Analysis
items.abstract_or_text: Anatomical stage is a principal determinant of treatment and prognosis in breast cancer, yet it is unclear how much information about stage is carried by the transcriptome of the primary tumour. We asked whether an a priori panel of 65 cancer-related genes can distinguish early-stage (AJCC Stage I-II) from late-stage (Stage III-IV) breast cancer, and which genes contribute to any signal. RNA-seq expression and pathologic stage for The Cancer Genome Atlas breast invasive carcinoma cohort (TCGA-BRCA) were obtained from the UCSC Xena platform. After restricting the data to primary tumours with a known stage, 1,075 tumours were analysed (805 early, 270 late) and split into stratified training (n = 860) and held-out test (n = 215) sets. Logistic regression, a support vector machine, random forest and gradient boosting were tuned by stratified five-fold cross-validation, with median imputation, standardisation and SMOTE oversampling fitted on training data only and classification thresholds chosen on out-of-fold training predictions. On the test set, Logistic Regression had the highest ROC-AUC, 0.618 (95% CI 0.530-0.704), with balanced accuracy 0.578, sensitivity 0.741 and specificity 0.416; differences in AUC between models were not statistically significant (DeLong p = 0.199-0.585). Permutation importance in the Gradient Boosting model ranked POU5F1, FLT3 and NOTCH1 highest, but this model's AUC confidence interval included 0.5, so the ranking is exploratory. No gene was differentially expressed between stage groups after false-discovery-rate (FDR) correction (smallest FDR = 0.057, CD44). A co-expression network built from training tumours identified REL, EP300 and ESR1 as the most connected genes, a property that reflects co-expression rather than regulation or association with stage. Limitations include a single cohort, no external validation, no clinical covariates and a small number of late-stage test tumours. Expression of this gene panel carries limited but measurable information about anatomical stage; expression-based stage models should be combined with clinicopathological variables and validated in independent cohorts before any clinical application is considered.

items.title: Development and Preliminary Evaluation of the Patient-Artificial Intelligence Rating Instrument
items.abstract_or_text: Importance: Patients increasingly use artificial intelligence (AI) for health-related conversations, but evaluation measures largely reflect clinician judgment. Objective: To develop and preliminarily evaluate a patient instrument assessing the quality of patient-AI health conversations. Design: Cross-sectional survey conducted June 5-14, 2026, following patient-partnered instrument development and cognitive interviews. Setting: An anonymous online survey. Participants: A convenience sample of adults with prior use of large language models for personal health-related queries, recruited from an academic medical center-affiliated Insight Panel and patient peers. Exposures: Participants' own prior health-related conversations with AI tools of their choosing. Main Outcomes and Measures: The Patient-AI Rating instrument comprised 12 communication-quality and patient engagement items rated from 1 to 5 and a separately scored patient-perceived-harm item. Internal consistency was assessed using Cronbach alpha, with sensitivity analyses using first ratings only for those using the tool to rate multiple conversations and participant-mean profiles. We examined item-total correlations, inter-item structure, and between- and within-participant variation. Results: Fourteen participants contributed 46 complete ratings; among 13 providing demographics, median age was 63 years (IQR, 53-70 years), and 8 (62%) reported female gender. Participants provided a median of 2 ratings (range, 1-17). Cronbach alpha was 0.88 (95% CI, 0.83-0.93) across all ratings, 0.85 using first ratings only, and 0.92 using participant-mean profiles. Corrected item-total correlations ranged from 0.42 to 0.72; mean inter-item correlation was 0.40. No item deletion improved Cronbach alpha. The mean quality score was 4.43 (SD, 0.45). Among 9 participants contributing multiple ratings, the intraclass correlation coefficient was 0.45, suggesting inter-conversation variability. No perceived harm was reported in 44 of 46 ratings (96%); the harm item correlated minimally with the instrument total (r = 0.09). Conclusions and Relevance: In this small cross-sectional study of engaged patients, the Patient-AI Rating instrument showed promising internal consistency and variation across rated conversations. These findings support further evaluation of patient-reported communication quality alongside clinician-based measures. Validation in larger, more diverse populations, including assessment of construct and criterion validity, is needed before broader use.

items.title: Development and internal validation of a prediction model for moderate-to-severe insomnia among nurses using machine learning-assisted predictor selection: a multicenter cross-sectional study
items.abstract_or_text: Abstract Background Clinically significant insomnia is common among nurses. We aimed to develop and internally validate a parsimonious prediction model for moderate-to-severe insomnia among nurses, to quantify its optimism, and to test whether machine learning adds value beyond logistic regression. Methods In a multicenter cross-sectional survey (four hospitals in China, 2023; N = 2,179), moderate-to-severe insomnia was defined as an Insomnia Severity Index (ISI) score ≥ 15. Candidate predictors were screened with Boruta and LASSO in a training set (n = 1,917), and a logistic regression model was evaluated in a stratified random test set (n = 262). Hospital identifiers were unavailable, so only internal validation was possible. Optimism was assessed with bootstrap correction, 500 repeated random splits and nested cross-validation including the selection step; random forest and gradient boosting served as benchmarks; calibration, net benefit and sensitivity to straight-line responding (n = 1,144 retained) were examined (TRIPOD + AI). Results Moderate-to-severe insomnia affected 29.8% (649/2,179). Night shifts per month, challenge and hindrance stress (CHSS) and career adaptability (CAAS) were selected in every nested fold: >8 night shifts/month versus none, odds ratio (OR) 2.37 (95% CI 1.79–3.15); hindrance stress per SD, 1.61 (1.35–1.93); challenge stress per SD, 1.33 (1.11–1.61); CAAS per 10 points, 0.84 (0.78–0.91). Test-set AUC was 0.766 (95% CI 0.708–0.825), calibration slope 1.36 (0.96–1.94) and Brier score 0.174; however, this lay in the upper range of 500 random splits (mean AUC 0.72; 2.5th–97.5th percentile 0.65–0.78), and the optimism-corrected AUC was 0.71 (nested cross-validation 0.71). Random forest (AUC 0.77) and gradient boosting (0.78) did not differ significantly from logistic regression, and the stress scales alone gave 0.75. At a risk threshold of 0.30, sensitivity was 72%, specificity 63% and positive predictive value 45%. Results were consistent in the screened subsample (AUC 0.72). Conclusions Night-shift burden, work stress and lower career adaptability were associated with moderate-to-severe insomnia, but discrimination was modest once optimism was accounted for (AUC about 0.71–0.72). Because predictors and outcome were self-reported at one time point and only internal validation was possible, the model and its nomogram are exploratory and require external validation before any use in practice.

items.title: Translational neuroscience in psychoeducation: Mapping nonmotor circuitry to clinical management in movement disorders
items.abstract_or_text: Non-motor symptoms (NMS) affect nearly all patients with Parkinson’s disease (PD)and related movement disorders, with a mean of roughly 8–10 discrete symptoms perindividual. Their effect on quality of life often exceeds that of motor features, yetNMS remain under-recognized and undertreated, partly because patients and caregivers lack a working model of why these symptoms arise in a “movement” disease.This chapter applies neuroscience-informed psychoeducation (NIPE) to that gap andpositions it relative to conventional psychoeducation, health communication, and behavioral science. We propose the Map-Normalize-Differentiate-Navigate (MNDN)workflow as a movement-disorders-specific implementation of the NIPE frameworkdescribed in Chapter 1 of this volume. MNDN is a clinical proposal, not a validatedprotocol: its components are specified so that it can be tested, but its effects on patient outcomes have not been evaluated. Drawing on the tripartite cortico-basal ganglia-thalamocortical loop model and multi-transmitter degeneration, we provide modules for seven high-yield NMS: apathy, anxiety, executive dysfunction, REM sleepbehavior disorder, neurogenic orthostatic hypotension, psychosis, and fatigue. Eachmodule summarizes the neural systems implicated, at the level of certainty the evidence supports, together with common misattributions, reversible contributors thatmust be excluded, management options and their limits, and patient and caregiverhandout content. We describe delivery formats from 3 to 5 min “micro-NIPE” sessions in routine visits to group and telehealth programs, specify the minimum components, provider competencies, dose, fidelity criteria, and proximal outcomes neededto test MNDN, and examine the ethical risks of neurobiological framing (determinism, oversimplification, over-attribution, and false reassurance), with particular attention to prognostic counseling in REM sleep behavior disorder. NIPE in movementdisorders is designed to reduce self-blame, support accurate symptom attribution, andimprove collaborative management. Whether it does so is an empirical question thatthis chapter aims to make answerable.
